links.note: Workers hostile to machines because they feared losing jobs and livelihood is 23890's description exactly (the Spinning Jenny episode). 23888 is why machines spread slowly from the industrialists' side; this item is the workers' side.

Seventeenth-century town merchants moving to the countryside to supply money to peasants and artisans producing for international markets is 23886 word for word. 23885 is the wider proto-industrialisation phenomenon; this item asks the merchants' specific purpose.

Which country industrialised first sits in the British industrialisation narrative that 23887 heads (cotton and metals leading the pace). DEFECT: the key is marked on 'Japan'. Britain is the first industrial country and is option (c) - the key is wrong.

Building activity in the cities - railway lines, stations, tunnels - opening employment is part of the abundant-cheap-labour argument in Victorian Britain, which is 23889 (industrialists preferring hand labour where labour was plentiful). The stem's 'after 1940s' is a typo for the 1840s. No separate 'life of the workers' concept exists in this frame.

Coarser cottons produced in many countries but the finer varieties coming from India is a sentence in the age-of-Indian-textiles passage, 23891. NOTE: the second option is labelled '(6)' instead of '(b)'.

Trade through the new ports of Bombay and Calcutta passing to European companies is the establishment of colonial commercial control, which 23893 heads. 23892 is the weavers' ruin that followed, and 23894 the shift to exporting raw material.

Three of the four names are the chapter's early Indian entrepreneurs (Dwarkanath Tagore, Seth Hukumchand, Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee); the invented one is the key. 23896 is the concept about who set up Indian industry and where their capital came from.
